source_text: CAPUT TERTIUM, De cognitione Dei; ubi ostenditur via, modus & ratio cognoscendi DEUM. Vidimus DEUM esse: nunc ostendemus viam, modum & rationem qua natura Dei a Christiano recte cognosci potest. Frustra enim quaerimus incognitum, nisi qua via & virtute investigandus sit praenoscimus. Natura illius cognosci nequit a priori: quia omnium prima est, Esa. 44.6; Apoc. 1.8. A Deo solo adaequate cognoscitur. A nobis cognoscitur quadamtenus, sed infinite inferius, 1 Cor. 13.12. Tertullianus: Nihil quicquam de Deo comprehendi potest, nisi quod sit incomprehensibilis. Augustinus: Deus hoc est, quod nulla attingit opinio.
english: CHAPTER THREE. On the knowledge of God; where the way, mode, and reason of knowing GOD are shown.

We have seen that GOD is: now we will show the way, mode, and reason by which God's nature can rightly be known by a Christian. For in vain we seek what is unknown unless we first know by what way and power it is to be investigated.

His nature cannot be known a priori, because it is first of all (Isaiah 44:6; Revelation 1:8). It is adequately known by God alone. By us it is known to some extent, but infinitely lower (1 Corinthians 13:12). Tertullian: nothing at all can be comprehended of God except that He is incomprehensible. Augustine: God is that which no opinion attains.

source_text: I. Cognoscitur autem Deus a nobis immediate aut mediate. II. Immediate, per visionem claram ejus sicuti est, 1 Joh. 3.2; 1 Cor. 13.12, & beatorum propria est in caelis. III. Mediate, per imagines analogicas & signa, quae sunt actiones Dei externae & opera & verbum ipsius, Psal. 19.1; Rom. 1.20. Haec cognitio per speculum in aenigmate dicitur, & viatorum propria est. IV. Mediate cognoscitur Deus ex operibus aut verbo tribus modis: affirmationis, negationis & supereminentiae. V. Primus modus est affirmationis. VI. Negationis modus removet imperfectiones; supereminentiae elevat perfectiones supra creaturarum modum.
english: I. Now God is known by us either immediately or mediately.
II. Immediately, by clear vision of Him as He is (1 John 3:2; 1 Corinthians 13:12), proper to the blessed in heaven.
III. Mediately, through analogical images and signs — God's outward actions, works, and word (Psalm 19:1; Romans 1:20). This knowledge is called through a mirror in an enigma, proper to pilgrims.

IV. Mediately God is known from His works or word in three modes: affirmation, negation, and eminence. V. The first mode is affirmation. VI. Negation removes imperfections; eminence raises perfections above the manner of creatures.

source_text: ASSERTIO PRIMA. Deus, sensu nostro exteriori, in se ac natura sua est imperceptus. Saepe in Scripturis legimus Deum visum esse; unde quis dubitet an oculis corporeis Deus cognosci possit? Id fieri non posse videtur, 1. ratione objecti: quia Deus incorporeus est & immensus; 2. ratione subjecti & organi: sensus non nisi per organa corporea cognoscit. Quapropter Esaias vidit speciem Dei sedentis, non Deum in se. Si oculi non vident Deum in se, multo minus alii sensus.
english: FIRST ASSERTION. God, by our outward sense, is imperceptible in Himself and in His nature.

Often in the Scriptures we read that God was seen; whence someone might doubt whether God can be known by bodily eyes. But that cannot be done: first, by reason of the object — God is incorporeal and immense; second, by reason of the subject and organ — sense knows only through bodily organs. Therefore Isaiah saw an appearance of God sitting, not God in Himself. If the eyes do not see God in Himself, much less do the other senses.

source_text: ASSERTIO SECUNDA. Deus naturali mentis nostrae discursu cognoscitur quidem, sed imperfectissimo modo. Cum sensu percipi non possit Deus, an ratione eum percipere possimus inquiremus. Multo languidius Deum cognoscimus ex effectis suis, qui a Deo infinite superantur. Hinc Nazianzenus, Platonem corrigens: Dei naturam nullis verbis explicari posse, animo atque intellectu comprehendi multo minus posse.
english: SECOND ASSERTION. God is indeed known by the natural discourse of our mind, but in a most imperfect way.

Since God cannot be perceived by sense, we inquire whether we can perceive Him by reason. But we know God much more faintly from His effects, which are infinitely surpassed by God. Hence Nazianzen, correcting Plato: God's nature can be explained by no words, and by mind and intellect can be comprehended still less.

source_text: ASSERTIO TERTIA. Deus, non per simulacrum quo essentia ipsius repraesentetur, sed intuitu celerimoque discursu mentis lumine gratiae corroboratae in hac vita cognosci potest. Hacpropter Paulus: Loquimur sapientiam Dei, quam nemo principum seculi cognovit, nobis autem revelavit Deus, 1 Cor. 2.7-10. Deus enim penitus ignota potest revelare per voces sensibiles, & notiones in nostro spiritu formare.
english: THIRD ASSERTION. God can be known in this life not through an image by which His essence would be represented, but by intuition and the swiftest discourse of a mind strengthened by the light of grace.

For this reason Paul says: we speak God's wisdom, which none of the rulers of this age knew, but God has revealed it to us (1 Corinthians 2:7-10). For God can reveal things thoroughly unknown through sensible words, and form notions in our spirit.

source_text: IX. E dictis est cognitionis Dei pressius observanda distinctio. X. Primò, alia est mediata, alia immediata. Illa in praesenti, haec in vita futura. XI. Secundò, illa est philosophica sive naturalis, aut vere theologica. Illa hauritur ex principiis naturae per discursum, estque rudis, obscura, angusta. Haec e Dei verbo percipitur, estque eruditior, planior, plenior. XII. Tertio, haec est theoretica aut practica. Illa mere historica & nuda; haec includit obedientiam verbo Dei praescriptam cum pietatis affectu & salutiferam.
english: IX. From what has been said a closer distinction of the knowledge of God is to be observed.
X. First, one is mediate, another immediate. That is in the present; this in the life to come.

XI. Second, that is philosophical or natural, or truly theological. That is drawn from nature's principles by discourse, and is rough, obscure, and narrow. This is perceived from God's word, and is more learned, plainer, and fuller.
XII. Third, this is theoretical or practical. That is merely historical and bare; this includes the obedience prescribed by God's word, joined with piety's affection and saving.

source_text: XIII. Usus cognitionis Dei his regulis continetur. 1. Etsi Deus a priori cognosci non potest, tamen a posteriori cognoscitur, Exod. 33.23. 2. Cognitio Dei implicita sola ad salutem nullius est momenti; oportet distincte cognoscere Deum unum & trinum, aeternum, omnipotentem, creatorem, redemtorem, sanctificatorem. 3. Cognitio aliqua Dei naturaliter insita est homini, quantum ad semen religionis. 4. Cognitio Dei naturalis sufficit ut sis inexcusalis, Rom. 1-2. 5. Cognitio Dei perfecta ad salutem integratur cognitione naturae, voluntatis & operum ejus. 6. Cognitio DEI tum demum salutaris est, quando est practica & filialis. 7. Cognitio Dei naturalis non interficitur, sed perficitur cognitione supra naturam. Nam liber naturae a libro Scripturae explicatur.
english: XIII. The use of the knowledge of God is contained in these rules.

1. Although God cannot be known a priori, yet He is known a posteriori (Exodus 33:23). 2. Implicit knowledge of God alone is of no moment for salvation; one must distinctly know God as one and three, eternal, almighty, creator, redeemer, sanctifier. 3. Some knowledge of God is naturally implanted as the seed of religion. 4. Natural knowledge of God suffices that you are without excuse (Romans 1-2). 5. Perfect knowledge of God for salvation is completed by knowledge of His nature, will, and works. 6. Knowledge of GOD is saving only when practical and filial. 7. Natural knowledge of God is not killed but perfected by knowledge above nature. For the book of nature is explained by the book of Scripture.
